rw: GDP adds up the market value of all final goods and services produced inside a country in a period, usually a year, which is exactly this definition.

ww.The total amount of exports only from th: Exports are only one part of a nation's output, and GDP counts everything produced at home, including goods and services sold domestically, so exports alone cannot be the total.
ww.The total money held by the government a: Money held by the government at the central bank is a balance sheet item and says nothing about how much the whole economy produces during a year.
ww.The total wages paid to workers in a cou: Wages paid to workers make up only part of income in an economy, and GDP measures total output value, which also includes profits, rents, and taxes.

rw: Supply and demand describes how the quantity sellers offer and the quantity buyers want both change with price, and the price settles where these two meet.

ww.A government plan to set all prices and: A government plan that sets all prices and wages describes central planning, not supply and demand, where prices move freely as buyers and sellers respond to each other.
ww.A list of items for sale in a store, wit: A list of items with prices and stock levels is just a store inventory sheet, and it does not explain how prices are set by buyers and sellers.
ww.A tax on goods sold abroad, paid by the: A tax on goods sold abroad is an export duty, which is a government policy tool and has nothing to do with how markets balance supply and demand.

rw: With more buyers competing for an unchanged supply, shortages push sellers to raise the price until the amount wanted again matches the amount available, so the price rises.

ww.It falls: If demand rises while supply stays fixed, more buyers chase the same goods, so sellers can charge more and the price does not fall.
ww.It is zero: A price of zero would only occur when a good is free and plentiful, which is the opposite of what happens when demand increases against fixed supply.
ww.No change: Prices respond to the balance of supply and demand, so a rise in demand with fixed supply must move the price, and it will not stay unchanged.

rw: A monopoly has a single seller and no close substitutes, so buyers have nowhere else to go, which gives the seller strong power over price.

ww.A market with many sellers of similar go: A market with many sellers of similar goods is described as competitive, and it is nearly the opposite of a monopoly, where only one seller exists.
ww.A market with a few large sellers and ma: A few large sellers and many buyers describes an oligopoly, in which several firms share the market, so it is not a monopoly, which has just one seller.
ww.A market owned by the customers and thei: A market owned by customers and their families describes a cooperative style of ownership and says nothing about the number of sellers or the lack of substitutes.

rw: Each month buys $100 divided by the price: 10 shares at $10, 20 shares at $5, then 10 shares at $10, and 10 plus 20 plus 10 equals 40 shares.

ww.30 shares: Thirty shares is wrong because it adds the prices incorrectly or counts only two months; the three purchases are 10 shares, 20 shares, and 10 shares, which total 40.
ww.25 shares: Twenty-five shares does not match any sum of the three purchases; $100 buys 10 shares at $10, 20 shares at $5, and 10 shares at $10, giving 40.
ww.20 shares: Twenty shares is only the purchase made in the cheap $5 month; it ignores the 10 shares bought in each of the other two months, so the total is really 40.

rw: With regular monthly contributions at a given return, compounding works longer on early deposits, so the length of time invested has the largest effect on the final balance.

ww.The day of the week you invest: The day of the week you invest has almost no effect over decades, because returns depend on growth over years and not on which weekday a deposit is made.
ww.The brand of your bank checkbook: The brand of a checkbook has no effect on investment growth, since the balance depends on contributions, returns, and time and not on the stationery you use.
ww.The color of the bank statement: The color of a bank statement is only cosmetic and cannot change returns, so it cannot affect how large the final balance becomes after years of saving.

rw: A target-date fund starts with more stocks for growth and gradually moves toward bonds and cash as the chosen retirement year approaches, lowering risk when it matters most.

ww.A fund that pays out all of its assets o: A target-date fund does not pay out all of its assets each year on a fixed date; it keeps investing and only slowly changes its mix of holdings over time.
ww.A fund that buys stocks only on the last: Buying stocks only on the last day of each month describes a trading schedule, but a target-date fund holds a mix of assets that is tied to a retirement year.
ww.A fund that invests only in companies ab: Investing only in companies about to go public describes a narrow, risky strategy, whereas a target-date fund holds broad stocks and bonds and adjusts the mix over time.

rw: Past performance does not guarantee future results, because markets change and luck plays a role, so chasing last year's winner can lead to disappointing returns.

ww.Top funds by law must repeat their resul: No law requires a top fund to repeat its results, and returns often fall back toward average the next year, so assuming repeat performance is a mistake.
ww.Top funds are always the safest choice f: Top funds are not always the safest, since high past returns can come from taking big risks, and those risks may produce large losses later.
ww.Top funds never charge any fees to their: Top funds still charge expense ratios and other fees, so claiming that they never charge fees is false and would not be a reason to choose them anyway.

rw: A stop-loss order automatically becomes a sell order once the price drops to the level you set, which limits how much you can lose on a position.

ww.An order to buy at the lowest price of t: Buying at the lowest price of the year would need perfect hindsight, and a stop-loss is a sell instruction, not a buy order, so this definition does not fit.
ww.An order that prevents all trades from b: A stop-loss order does not block trading; it is a specific instruction placed with a broker, and it only triggers a sale when the stated price is reached.
ww.An order to buy when prices rise by a se: An order to buy after prices rise by a set amount is a buy-stop order, whereas a stop-loss is a sell order that triggers when prices fall.

rw: Margin investing means borrowing money from a broker to buy more securities than your cash would allow, which magnifies both potential gains and potential losses on the position.

ww.Investing only your own cash and none bo: Using only your own cash with no borrowing is the opposite of margin investing, which by definition involves a loan from the broker to buy securities.
ww.Investing on the edges of the market for: Margin has nothing to do with the edges of the market or small price moves; it refers to a loan from a broker used to purchase securities.
ww.Investing in a savings account at a loca: Putting money in a savings account at a local bank is ordinary saving, and it involves no borrowing from a broker, so it is not margin investing.

rw: Because the broker's loan must be repaid in full, a sharp price drop can cause losses larger than the original investment, which is the main risk of margin.

ww.Margin loans are free of any interest ch: Margin loans do charge interest, so calling them free is false, and the interest cost adds to the losses an investor may face on a falling position.
ww.Your losses are capped at ten percent: Losses are not capped at ten percent; because you borrow to buy more, a fall in price can wipe out your money and leave you owing more.
ww.The broker guarantees your profit each t: Brokers never guarantee profits on margin trades; they lend money and expect repayment with interest whether the investment gains or loses, so the investor carries all the risk.

rw: A ticker symbol is a short code of letters that identifies a listed company or fund when orders are placed and prices are quoted on the exchange.

ww.A rating for the company's debt load: A rating of a company's debt load comes from credit rating agencies, while a ticker symbol is just a short code used to name the stock in markets.
ww.A tax number for the company's filings: A tax number used on a company's filings is an identification number for tax authorities, and it is a different thing from the short letters used in trading.
ww.A password to log in to a broker's site: A ticker symbol is a public code for a stock, not a password, and it gives no access to anyone's broker account or login.

rw: NAV is found by subtracting the fund's liabilities from its assets and dividing by the number of shares, giving the per-share value at which mutual fund shares trade.

ww.The yearly fee of the fund and its manag: A yearly fee to hold a fund is its expense ratio, not NAV, which instead measures the value of one share based on the fund's assets and liabilities.
ww.The total number of investors in the fun: The number of investors in a fund is a count of shareholders and has no role in the NAV calculation, which uses assets, liabilities, and shares outstanding.
ww.The price printed on a stock certificate: A price printed on a stock certificate is the par or original issue figure for a stock, and a mutual fund's NAV is recalculated each day from its holdings.

rw: Index funds hold hundreds of companies in one fund and charge very low fees, so investors get wide diversification at low cost, which suits long-term goals.

ww.They are insured by the government again: Index funds are not insured against loss by the government; FDIC insurance covers bank deposits, while fund values rise and fall with the markets they track.
ww.They carry no market risk as they hold m: Holding many stocks reduces company-specific risk but not market risk, so an index fund can still fall sharply when the whole market declines.
ww.They guarantee that they will beat the m: An index fund aims to match the market, not beat it, so no guarantee of outperformance exists, and it will rise and fall roughly in line with its index.

rw: Volatility describes how much and how quickly a price swings up and down, with higher volatility meaning bigger and faster changes and therefore more uncertainty for holders.

ww.How long the company has existed, counte: The age of a company in years has no link to volatility, since young and old firms can both have stable or wildly moving share prices.
ww.How much dividend it pays out to holders: Dividends paid to holders are called the dividend, and volatility measures price movement, so how much a company pays out does not define volatility.
ww.How many shares exist in the whole marke: The number of shares in the whole market is not a measure of price movement, so it does not describe volatility, which is about swings in price.

rw: An aggressive portfolio puts a high share in stocks, accepting larger swings and the chance of bigger losses in exchange for higher expected long-term growth.

ww.A high share of cash and short-term bond: A high share of cash and short-term bonds is a cautious, low-risk mix and describes a conservative portfolio, which is the opposite of aggressive.
ww.Only government bonds and cash funds: Only government bonds and cash funds is among the most cautious setups available, so it is a conservative approach and not an aggressive one seeking growth.
ww.Only insured savings accounts at banks: Insured savings accounts are very safe and earn little, so a portfolio made only of them is conservative and does not aim for the growth that aggressive portfolios seek.

rw: A conservative portfolio holds more bonds and cash so that the original amount invested is less likely to fall, accepting lower growth in return for stability.

ww.Mostly new company stocks bought for rap: New company stocks bought for rapid growth describe an aggressive, risk-seeking approach, which is the opposite of a conservative portfolio that aims to protect savings.
ww.Mostly speculative stocks of young firms: Speculative stocks of young firms carry a high risk of loss, so a portfolio made of them is aggressive and does not match a conservative goal.
ww.Mostly options contracts on shares and b: Options contracts are complex and risky instruments that can lose all their value quickly, so a portfolio mostly made of them would not be conservative.

rw: With ten years to go, a mix of stocks and bonds gives some growth, and moving gradually toward safer holdings as the purchase date nears protects the money.

ww.All in one start-up company that has no: Putting everything in one start-up with no profits or sales is extreme concentration, so a single failure could erase the savings needed for the home purchase.
ww.All in speculative stocks until the mone: All speculative stocks until the money is needed risks a large loss right before the purchase, with no time to recover, which is unsuitable for a ten year goal.
ww.All in cash for the whole ten years unti: All cash for ten years is safe from market drops but may lose purchasing power to inflation, so it gives up growth that a ten year horizon can capture.

rw: The saying means spreading money across many different investments, so that if one performs badly, the others can offset the loss and the overall risk falls.

ww.Never invest any money: The saying does not tell you to avoid investing; it advises spreading your money across several assets so that no single loss can sink your savings.
ww.Invest only in food companies: Food companies are not what the saying points to, since eggs are only a metaphor for money, and it recommends variety across many different kinds of holdings.
ww.Spend your money on eggs: The eggs are a metaphor, not a literal suggestion to buy eggs, and the advice concerns splitting investments among assets and not about spending on groceries.

rw: Social media tips can be false, paid promotions, or part of pump-and-dump schemes, so acting on one without research can lead to large and quick losses.

ww.Tips are guaranteed by regulators, so no: Regulators do not guarantee social media tips, and many tips are unverified or false, so the claim that nobody can lose is wrong and dangerous.
ww.Tips are illegal to read or to pass on t: Reading or sharing a tip is not illegal in itself; the risk is that the tip may be misleading, promotional, or a scheme meant to trap investors.
ww.Tips are always accurate and come from e: Tips online are often wrong and come from people with no expertise or hidden interests, so assuming they are always accurate and expert is a costly mistake.

rw: Dividend reinvestment uses the dividends paid out to buy additional shares, which grows the number of shares owned and lets future dividends compound over time.

ww.Spending dividends on bills and food: Spending dividends on bills and food is using them as income and does not reinvest them, because reinvesting means putting the money back into the investment.
ww.Returning dividends to the company: Returning dividends to the company would cancel the payout and is not reinvestment, which buys more shares for the investor and not for the company.
ww.Sending dividends to a charity: Sending dividends to a charity is a donation of the income, so the investor gets no extra shares and it is not dividend reinvestment.

rw: The bond has a face value of $1,000 and was bought for $950, which is less than face value, and buying below face value is called buying at a discount.

ww.Buying on margin: Buying on margin means borrowing from a broker to buy securities, and it has nothing to do with paying less than face value for a bond.
ww.Buying at a premium: A premium means paying more than the $1,000 face value, but $950 is below that amount, so this purchase is not at a premium.
ww.Buying at par value: Buying at par means paying exactly the $1,000 face value, but $950 is $50 lower, so this is not a purchase at par.

rw: Yield measures the income an investment returns, such as interest or dividends, as a percent of its price or cost, which lets investors compare different investments.

ww.The fee a broker charges for each trade: A fee charged by a broker for executing a trade is a commission, which is a cost and not the income an investment returns as a percent of price.
ww.The total number of shares an investor o: The total number of shares an investor owns is their holding or position size, and it says nothing about the income earned as a percent of price.
ww.The date a bond matures and the principa: The date a bond matures and repays principal is its maturity date, and it is different from yield, which measures income relative to the investment's price.

rw: Saving keeps money safe and easy to reach for near-term needs, while investing accepts the chance of loss in order to seek growth over a longer time.

ww.Saving has more risk than investing, sin: Saving is generally the lower risk choice, such as an insured bank account, so saying it has more risk than investing reverses the real relationship.
ww.Investing is the same as saving, with th: Saving and investing differ in risk, access, and expected return, so claiming they are the same in every way ignores real differences that matter for planning.
ww.Saving always earns more than investing: Saving does not always earn more; over long periods, investments in stocks have usually earned higher returns than savings accounts, although with more risk.

rw: Stocks are 80 percent of the portfolio, so a 10 percent drop costs 0.80 times 10, which is 8 percent, while the unchanged bonds add no loss.

ww.About 2 percent: Two percent would come from 20 percent times 10 percent, which applies the stock drop to the bond share, but it is stocks that fell, and they are 80 percent.
ww.About 18 percent: Eighteen percent comes from adding 8 and 10, which double counts; only the stock portion fell, and 80 percent times 10 percent gives just 8 percent.
ww.About 10 percent: A 10 percent portfolio loss would need every holding to fall 10 percent, but bonds were unchanged and are 20 percent of the portfolio, so the loss is only 8 percent.

rw: Each trade can bring commissions, spreads, and taxes on short-term gains, which reduce the net return, so more trading often leaves investors with less money.

ww.It is not legal to do so: Frequent trading is legal, so it is not true that it is against the law, although it may cost investors more money than they expect.
ww.It removes all risk of loss: Trading does not remove risk; every trade still exposes the investor to price changes, and frequent trading can add costs on top of the existing risk.
ww.It always lifts returns for you: Frequent trading does not always lift returns, since costs and mistimed trades can reduce them, and studies show active traders often earn less than buy-and-hold investors.

rw: Comparing prices and quality across stores or brands helps a shopper find the best value for their money, and this saving is why the habit is smart.

ww.It is required by law for shoppers: No law requires shoppers to compare prices; it is a personal habit people adopt because it saves money, so legal requirement is not the reason it is smart.
ww.It guarantees the lowest price in the wo: Comparison shopping cannot guarantee the lowest price in the world, because nobody can check every seller, but it does improve the chance of a good deal.
ww.It removes the need for a budget plan: A budget is still needed because comparison shopping only affects the price of each purchase, and it does not control the total amount that you spend.

rw: Dividing $4.20 by 24 ounces gives $0.175 per ounce, which is lower than the $0.20 per ounce for the smaller bottle, so the 24 oz size is better value.

ww.The 16 oz bottle at $0.20 an ounce, the: The 16 oz bottle costs $3.20 divided by 16, which is $0.20 an ounce, and that is higher than the larger bottle's unit price, so it is not the better buy.
ww.The 16 oz bottle because it costs less i: Total cost is the wrong measure, since the smaller bottle holds less; per ounce it costs $0.20, which is more than the $0.175 for the larger bottle.
ww.They are the same price per ounce in tot: The unit prices differ: $3.20 divided by 16 is $0.20 per ounce, while $4.20 divided by 24 is $0.175 per ounce, so they are not equal.

rw: Adding the $4 item brings the total to $50, the coupon cuts it to $40, so she pays less than $46, but this helps only if she wanted the item.

ww.Yes always, as coupons are free money an: Coupons are not free money if you buy something you do not need; adding a $4 item just to save $10 means spending more than before, so always is wrong.
ww.No, because coupons cannot be used on pu: The coupon requires a purchase of $50 or more, so it can be used at $50 and above; saying it cannot be used there reverses the rule.
ww.Yes, because the item becomes free of ch: The item is not free; she still pays $40 for $50 of goods, so the extra $4 item is only partly offset by the coupon and costs her real money.

rw: Buying on impulse means purchasing something without planning ahead, often on a sudden urge, rather than because the item was on a list or budget.

ww.Purchasing at a discount: A discount describes the price of an item and not the reason for buying, since people can plan purchases of discounted goods, so it is not an impulse buy.
ww.Purchasing only listed items: Purchasing only listed items is the opposite of impulse buying, because sticking to a shopping list is a planned approach to spending.
ww.Purchasing online or in store: Shopping online or in a store describes where someone buys and not why, so both can be planned or impulsive and neither defines buying on impulse.

rw: Basic groceries supply the food a person must eat to live and stay healthy, so they are a need and not simply something that is wanted.

ww.A concert ticket: A concert ticket is entertainment, which is nice to have but not required for survival or basic living, so it is a want and not a need.
ww.A new video game: A new video game is a leisure purchase that people can live without, so it is classified as a want and not as a basic need.
ww.A streaming plan: A streaming plan provides entertainment that is optional, so it counts as a want, and households can survive and function without paying for it.

rw: A trade-off means giving up one thing to get another, and since money is limited, buying one item often means you cannot afford the second item.

ww.Returning an item and taking a full refu: Returning an item for a full refund is a purchase return, and a trade-off is about giving up one choice to afford another, not about refunds.
ww.Getting both items for free from the sho: Getting both items free from a shop involves no sacrifice, whereas a trade-off always means giving something up, such as an alternative purchase.
ww.Trading with friends only, swapping good: Swapping goods with friends is barter and is not what a trade-off means in a purchase decision, where you give up one option for another.

rw: An emergency fund exists to cover surprise costs such as repairs or medical bills, so using it avoids debt and keeps your regular budget on track.

ww.Ignore it for a while: Ignoring an unplanned expense usually makes it worse, as late fees, damage, or health problems can grow, so delaying the response is not a good plan.
ww.Pay it with a card: Paying with a card may lead to interest charges and debt if the balance is not cleared, so it is a weaker choice than using savings set aside.
ww.Skip your other bills: Skipping other bills causes late fees, damaged credit, and possible service cutoffs, which creates new problems instead of solving the original unexpected expense.

rw: A longer loan term lowers the monthly payment but adds more interest over time, and fees add further cost, so total cost can be much higher than expected.

ww.Monthly payments are never important at: Monthly payments matter a great deal for budgeting, so saying they never matter is false, but they alone hide the full amount a loan will cost.
ww.Lenders never charge any fees of any kin: Lenders often charge fees such as origination or closing costs, so saying they never charge any fees is false and is not a reason to compare total costs.
ww.Total cost is always equal to the monthl: Total cost is the sum of all payments plus fees, which usually exceeds the monthly payment many times over, so the two are not equal.

rw: Ten percent of $200,000 is 0.10 times 200,000, which equals $20,000, so that is the required down payment on the home.

ww.$2,000: Two thousand dollars is only one percent of $200,000, so it understates the down payment; ten percent is ten times larger at $20,000.
ww.$200,000: The full price of $200,000 is 100 percent of the home's value, but the question asks only for the ten percent down payment, which is $20,000.
ww.$180,000: One hundred eighty thousand dollars is the amount left to borrow after a $20,000 down payment, and not the down payment itself.

rw: Equity equals the home's value minus the mortgage balance, so $300,000 minus $210,000 equals $90,000, which is the part of the home the owner holds.

ww.$210,000: The mortgage balance of $210,000 is what the owner still owes, and equity is the home's value minus that balance, so it is not the equity.
ww.$30,000: Thirty thousand dollars does not follow from the figures; subtracting $210,000 from $300,000 gives $90,000, and $30,000 is only the difference of unrelated numbers.
ww.$510,000: Adding the value and the balance to get $510,000 is a mistake, because equity is found by subtracting what is owed from what the home is worth.

rw: Closing costs are the fees and expenses, such as title, appraisal, and lender charges, that buyers pay when finalizing a home purchase, in addition to the down payment.

ww.The cost of closing a bank account, char: Closing a bank account is a different event; closing costs refer to the fees paid at the finalizing of a real estate purchase and not to ending an account.
ww.The monthly mortgage payment on a home o: The monthly mortgage payment is a recurring bill paid after the purchase, whereas closing costs are one-time fees paid when the sale is finalized.
ww.The cost of moving boxes and packing tap: Moving boxes and tape are costs of relocating, and they are not part of the fees due at the closing of the home purchase.

rw: A security deposit is held to cover damage or unpaid rent, so when the apartment is left in good condition it should generally be returned, minus lawful deductions.

ww.The landlord keeps it whatever state the: A landlord cannot keep a deposit just because he wants to; it generally must be returned when the unit is left in good condition, apart from lawful deductions.
ww.It is turned into rent for the next mont: A deposit is not automatically converted into next month's rent, and tenants who leave are entitled to its return, unless there is damage or unpaid rent.
ww.It is given to the government as a tax o: A deposit is the tenant's money held by the landlord, not a tax or a government fee, so it is not handed over to the government.

rw: Interest is the price paid for using someone else's money, such as a borrower paying a lender, or a bank paying a depositor for holding funds.

ww.A tax paid on income earned each year: A tax paid on income is a tax, not interest, which is the cost of borrowing money or the payment received for lending it.
ww.A fee for opening a bank account today: A fee for opening a bank account is a service charge, whereas interest is the amount paid for the use of money borrowed or deposited.
ww.The value of shares held at year end: The value of shares held at year end is the market value of an investment, and it is not interest, which is a payment for using money.

rw: When rates rise, new bonds pay more, so older bonds with lower fixed rates are less attractive and their market prices tend to fall until their yields compete.

ww.They double in value: Existing bond prices do not double after a rate increase; buyers prefer newer bonds with higher rates, so older lower-rate bonds lose value instead of gaining.
ww.They tend to rise: Prices of older bonds rise when rates fall, not when they rise, since a bond with a higher fixed rate is worth more then; the reverse happens here.
ww.They stay the same: Bond prices are linked to interest rates, so a sharp increase in rates changes the value of older bonds, which means their prices do not stay the same.

rw: Inflation raises prices over time, so each unit of money buys less, which means it erodes the purchasing power of money.

ww.The date a bond matures soon: A bond's maturity date is fixed in its terms and inflation does not change it, so inflation does not erode the date a bond matures.
ww.The face value written on a bond: The face value written on a bond is a fixed number of dollars, and inflation does not alter it, but it lowers what that sum can buy.
ww.The number of shares owned: The number of shares owned stays the same during inflation unless the owner buys or sells; inflation affects what money can buy, not share counts.

rw: The Rule of 72 estimates doubling time by dividing 72 by the annual rate, so 72 divided by 6 equals 12 years for the investment to double.

ww.6 years: Six years is just the interest rate, not the doubling time; the Rule of 72 divides 72 by the rate, so 72 divided by 6 gives 12.
ww.24 years: Twenty-four years would be the doubling time at a 3 percent rate, because 72 divided by 3 is 24, while at 6 percent it is shorter.
ww.72 years: Seventy-two is the constant in the rule and not the answer; you divide 72 by the rate of 6 percent, which gives 12 years to double.

rw: Liquidity describes how quickly an asset can be converted into cash without a loss in value, so cash is highly liquid while real estate is less so.

ww.The amount of risk that is built into an: The amount of risk built into an investment is called its risk level, and liquidity instead measures how easily it can be converted to cash.
ww.The amount of interest that an investmen: The amount of interest an investment pays each year is its yield or interest rate, which is different from how quickly it can be sold for cash.
ww.The amount of tax that is owed on an inv: The tax owed when an investment is sold is a capital gains tax, and liquidity has nothing to do with taxes but with ease of selling.

rw: The real rate of return takes the nominal return and subtracts inflation, showing how much the buying power of an investment actually grew over the period.

ww.The return before any fees or taxes appl: Return before fees or taxes is the gross return, and the real rate of return is different, since it adjusts the return for the effect of inflation.
ww.The highest return an investment has eve: The highest return an investment has ever had is its peak return, which says nothing about how inflation affects the purchasing power of the earnings.
ww.The interest rate set by the central ban: The central bank sets a policy interest rate, but it is not the real return, which is an investment's nominal return after removing inflation.

rw: The real return is the nominal return minus inflation, so 3 percent minus 4 percent equals negative 1 percent, meaning the investor lost a little purchasing power.

ww.Positive 7 percent: Positive 7 percent adds the 3 percent return and the 4 percent inflation, but inflation should be subtracted, so the real return is not 7 percent.
ww.Positive 1 percent: A positive 1 percent would result from subtracting in the wrong direction, taking 4 minus 3, whereas the earnings of 3 percent fell short of inflation by 1.
ww.Zero percent overall: Zero percent would require the return to match the 4 percent inflation exactly, but the investment earned only 3 percent, which leaves a real loss of 1.

rw: A stock exchange is a marketplace where buyers and sellers trade securities such as stocks under set rules, which gives investors a transparent place to deal.

ww.A company that issues all of the stocks: A stock exchange does not issue all of a nation's stocks; companies issue their own shares, and the exchange only provides the place to trade them.
ww.A government agency that taxes trading a: Exchanges are not government agencies that tax trading or set prices, because prices come from buyers and sellers placing orders in the market.
ww.A bank that lends money to investors and: An exchange does not lend money to investors; banks and brokers do that, while the exchange provides the market where securities change hands.

rw: A first sale of shares to the public in an IPO is a primary market event because the company receives the money from the sale of new shares.

ww.The forex market: The forex market trades currencies and has nothing to do with a company selling its shares to the public for the first time.
ww.The commodities market: The commodities market deals in goods such as oil, wheat, and metals, and a company selling its own shares in an IPO is a different market.
ww.The secondary market: The secondary market is where investors trade existing shares among themselves after the IPO, and the company gets no new money from those trades.

rw: A bull market is a period of rising prices, often with investor confidence and strong economic news, which is the standard meaning of the term.

ww.A market closed for the day: A market closed for the day is simply a closed market and has nothing to do with bull markets, which are about the direction of prices.
ww.A market for farm animals only: Bull markets are about rising securities prices and not about farm animals, so a market for livestock does not match the finance term.
ww.A period when prices are falling: A period when prices are falling describes a bear market, which is the opposite of a bull market, where prices are rising.

rw: A bear market is commonly defined as a decline of 20 percent or more from recent highs, which marks a deep and lasting fall in prices.

ww.5 percent: A drop of 5 percent is a normal pullback that happens often and is not enough to count as a bear market, which needs a larger decline.
ww.2 percent: A decline of 2 percent is a small daily or weekly move that is common in markets, far smaller than the size that defines a bear market.
ww.50 percent: A fall of 50 percent is a severe crash that would be well beyond a bear market, since the usual threshold is a 20 percent decline.

rw: The New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq are the two largest U.S. stock exchanges, where thousands of companies list shares that investors buy and sell.

ww.IRS and FBI: The IRS and the FBI are government agencies, one for taxes and one for law enforcement, and neither is a stock exchange where shares are traded.
ww.FDIC and SEC: The FDIC insures bank deposits and the SEC regulates securities markets, and neither is an exchange where investors trade shares of companies.
ww.WTO and IMF: The WTO oversees world trade rules and the IMF supports global finance, and neither is a U.S. stock exchange, so this pair is wrong.

rw: A market order buys or sells immediately at the best price available at that moment, which favors speed over a guaranteed price.

ww.Sets the price for all buyers and seller: A market order does not set a price for all participants, since prices come from many buyers and sellers, and it just takes the current price.
ww.Cancels all trades made earlier in the d: An order cannot cancel the trades of others; a market order only affects your own trade, which executes against orders that are already in the market.
ww.Waits for a stated price before the trad: Waiting for a stated price describes a limit order, whereas a market order is carried out right away at whatever price the market offers.

rw: A limit order lets you name a price, so a buy executes only at that price or lower and a sell only at that price or higher.

ww.Limits how many shares exist in a compan: A limit order does not control how many shares a company has; it sets the price at which you are willing to trade your own shares.
ww.Stops a company from issuing more shares: Companies decide on issuing shares through their boards and shareholders, and a limit order from an investor has no power to stop that process.
ww.Buys immediately at any price on the mar: Buying immediately at any available price describes a market order, which is the opposite of a limit order that insists on your chosen price.

rw: The P/E ratio equals price per share divided by earnings per share, showing how many dollars investors pay for each dollar of yearly profit.

ww.Dividend per share: Dividing price by dividend per share gives the inverse of the dividend yield and not the P/E ratio, which compares price with profits.
ww.Book value per share: Price divided by book value per share is the price-to-book ratio, a different measure from the P/E ratio, which uses earnings in the denominator.
ww.Number of shares: Dividing price by the number of shares makes no sense, since price is already per share, and the P/E ratio uses earnings per share.

rw: Earnings per share equal net income divided by shares outstanding, so $2 million divided by 1 million shares equals $2.00 for each share.

ww.$1.00: One dollar would be correct only if net income were $1 million; with $2 million of income and 1 million shares, the result is higher.
ww.$3.00: Three dollars would need $3 million of net income with 1 million shares, but the company earned only $2 million, so the result is $2.00.
ww.$0.50: Fifty cents would result from dividing the income by 4 million shares or halving it, but dividing $2 million by 1 million shares gives $2.00.

rw: Dividend yield equals the annual dividend divided by the share price, so $2 divided by $50 equals 0.04, or 4 percent.

ww.25 percent: Twenty-five percent would need a dividend of $12.50 on a $50 stock, but a $2 dividend divided by $50 is much smaller than that.
ww.40 percent: Forty percent would need a $20 dividend on a $50 stock, which is far above the $2 paid, so it overstates the yield by a factor of ten.
ww.2 percent: Two percent would result from dividing $2 by $100, but the stock trades at $50, so the right calculation of $2 over $50 gives 4 percent.

rw: Beta measures a stock's volatility relative to the overall market, so a beta above 1 means bigger swings than the market and below 1 means smaller.

ww.How much the company pays out in dividen: Dividends paid out each year are measured by the dividend rate or yield, whereas beta describes how a stock's price moves relative to the overall market.
ww.The number of shares outstanding at the: The number of shares outstanding is a count of shares in existence and is unrelated to beta, which compares price swings with the market.
ww.The age of the company in years since fo: The age of a company since its founding is not captured by beta, which is a statistical measure of price movement compared with the market.

rw: Fundamental analysis studies a company's financial statements, earnings, management, and industry to estimate what the business is truly worth and where it may be heading.

ww.Only the price charts of the company's o: Studying only price charts of a stock is technical analysis, whereas fundamental analysis looks at the business itself, such as profits, debts, and growth prospects.
ww.The weather in the cities where a compan: Weather in cities where a company operates is not a core input, though it might matter for a few businesses, and it is not what fundamental analysis studies.
ww.Social media trends about the company's: Social media trends may reflect sentiment but are not the core subject of fundamental analysis, which examines a company's financial health and business outlook.

rw: Technical analysis studies past price patterns and trading volume on charts to predict where a price may go next, without relying on company financials.

ww.A company's management quality: Management quality is judged through fundamental analysis of the business, whereas technical analysis relies on price and volume data and not on judgments about managers.
ww.The company's product reviews: Product reviews relate to the business and its customers, which belong to fundamental analysis, and technical analysis ignores them in favor of market data.
ww.Government tax rules and laws: Government tax rules are economic and legal factors that fundamental analysis may consider, but technical analysis focuses on charts of price and volume.

rw: Total return combines the change in price with dividends or interest received, giving the complete picture of what an investment earned over the period.

ww.Price change only, with no dividends: Price change only, with no dividends, leaves out income received by the holder, so it is the price return and not the total return.
ww.Dividends only, with no change in the pr: Dividends only, with no price change, ignores any gain or loss in the share price, so it is the income return and not the total return.
ww.The investor's tax bill for the year: An investor's tax bill is a cost that depends on personal circumstances, and it is not a component of total return, which counts price change and income.

rw: Risk tolerance describes how much loss in the value of investments an investor is able and willing to accept without abandoning the plan.

ww.The fees an investor pays to a broker ea: Fees paid to a broker each year are a cost of investing, and they do not define risk tolerance, which is about how much loss you can accept.
ww.The number of investments an investor ow: The number of investments an investor owns is a measure of diversification and not risk tolerance, which concerns comfort with possible losses.
ww.How much an investor earns each year in: How much an investor earns each year is income, and it does not describe risk tolerance, which is about the ability to accept investment losses.

rw: A person in her twenties has decades before retirement, so she can ride out market drops and reasonably hold a larger share of stocks for growth.

ww.Only a short-term CD: Only a short-term CD is very safe but grows slowly, which wastes the long time horizon and high risk tolerance that favor stocks for growth.
ww.Only cash under a mattress: Cash under a mattress earns nothing and loses buying power to inflation, so it is a poor choice for a long horizon and is not reasonable.
ww.Only short-term savings: Short-term savings protect money needed soon, but for a long time horizon with high risk tolerance, keeping only these gives up valuable growth.

rw: Asset allocation divides a portfolio among asset classes such as stocks, bonds, and cash to balance risk and return according to goals and time horizon.

ww.Choosing a single stock to buy and holdi: Choosing a single stock and holding it is concentration in one asset, which is the opposite of dividing money among different asset classes.
ww.Paying fees to a broker for each trade m: Paying a broker fee for each trade describes a transaction cost and not allocation, which is about how you split money among asset classes.
ww.Selling all investments in a portfolio a: Selling everything and holding only cash is a decision to leave the market, whereas asset allocation divides a portfolio among several types of assets.

rw: Rebalancing means buying and selling so that holdings return to the target allocation, which controls risk after some assets have grown faster than others.

ww.Never changing the portfolio once it is: Never changing the portfolio is the opposite of rebalancing, which requires periodic adjustments to bring holdings back to the planned mix.
ww.Buying only the best performer of the ye: Buying only the best performer of the year concentrates risk and ignores the target mix, which is not what rebalancing aims to do.
ww.Selling everything you own and restartin: Selling everything and restarting fresh is a full reset that triggers costs and taxes, while rebalancing only adjusts holdings back toward the planned allocation.

rw: Cash in a savings account can be withdrawn immediately at full value, which makes it the most liquid of these choices.

ww.A collectible painting: A collectible painting can take time to sell and its price is uncertain, so it is far less liquid than cash in a savings account.
ww.A 30-year bond held to term: A 30-year bond held to term is tied up for decades, and selling early may mean a loss, so it is less liquid than a savings balance.
ww.A piece of land to hold: Land can take months or years to sell, with significant costs and uncertain prices, so a piece of land is a very illiquid asset.

rw: Near retirement there is less time to recover from losses, so investors usually shift toward lower-risk assets that produce steady income, such as bonds.

ww.Higher-risk growth stocks only, for big: Holding only high-risk growth stocks near retirement exposes savings to a large drop with little time to recover, so it is not typical.
ww.Speculative short-term trades each day: Speculative daily trading adds risk and costs, and it does not suit an investor who wants to protect savings as retirement approaches.
ww.Borrowing to invest even more funds: Borrowing to invest increases risk and creates debt that must be repaid, which is the wrong direction for someone who needs to preserve savings.

rw: The expense ratio is the annual cost of running a fund, such as management fees and expenses, shown as a percent of the fund's assets.

ww.The fund's yearly return as a percent of: A fund's yearly return as a percent of its share price describes performance, while the expense ratio shows what the fund charges to operate.
ww.The tax that is paid on the gains made b: Taxes paid on gains are a separate matter that depends on the investor and the fund's activity, and they are not what an expense ratio measures.
ww.The number of different holdings that th: The number of holdings in a fund relates to diversification and has no link to the expense ratio, which measures the yearly cost as a percent.

rw: The Securities and Exchange Commission is the federal agency that regulates the securities markets, enforces laws against fraud, and protects investors in the United States.

ww.Federal Trade Commission agency: The Federal Trade Commission focuses on consumer protection and competition in commerce, and it does not regulate the securities markets, which is the job of the SEC.
ww.Internal Revenue Service agency: The Internal Revenue Service collects federal taxes and enforces tax law, and it does not regulate how securities are issued and traded.
The Food and Drug Administration regulates food, drugs, and medical products, so it has no role in overseeing the securities markets in the United States.

rw: FINRA is a self-regulatory organization that writes and enforces rules for brokerage firms and registered brokers, working under the oversight of the SEC.

ww.A bank that insures the deposits of its: An institution that insures deposits up to a limit describes the FDIC, and FINRA is a different organization that oversees brokerage firms and their brokers.
ww.A stock exchange where shares are bought: A stock exchange is a place for trading shares, and FINRA does not run such a market; it regulates the firms and people who sell securities.
ww.A federal tax agency that collects incom: Collecting income taxes from workers and firms is the job of the IRS, whereas FINRA oversees securities firms and brokers and does not collect taxes.

rw: A fiduciary must act in the client's best interest, putting that interest ahead of their own and avoiding conflicts, which is the core of the duty.

ww.Guarantee a minimum return rate: A fiduciary cannot promise a minimum return, since no investment can guarantee one; the legal duty is to put the client's interests first.
ww.Avoid telling clients about risks: A fiduciary must disclose risks and conflicts honestly, so avoiding telling clients about risks would break the duty instead of meeting it.
ww.Maximize the firm's profit above all: Maximizing the firm's profit above all would put the firm's interests first, but a fiduciary must put the client's interests ahead of the firm's.

rw: Insider trading is illegal because trading on material nonpublic information gives some traders an unfair advantage over the public, which undermines trust and fairness in the markets.

ww.It involves buying too many shares in on: Buying many shares of one company is not illegal and does not by itself raise prices improperly; insider trading depends on using secret information to trade.
ww.It means that an investor trades through: Trading through a broker is the normal way investors buy and sell securities and is perfectly legal, so it is not what makes insider trading illegal.
ww.It means holding a stock for the long te: Holding a stock for the long term is a normal strategy and entirely legal, which means it is not what makes insider trading a crime.

rw: A stockbroker buys and sells securities on behalf of clients, carries out their orders, and often gives advice, earning commissions or fees for the service.

ww.Writes securities laws for the U.S. Cong: Writing securities laws is the job of Congress and regulators, whereas a stockbroker carries out orders for clients and does not make the laws.
ww.Audits companies' books for the governme: Auditing company books is done by accountants and auditors, and stockbrokers have no such role, since they handle the trading of securities for clients.
ww.Sets the interest rate for the whole eco: Setting interest rates for the whole economy is done by the central bank, not by stockbrokers, who work with clients on individual securities trades.

rw: SIPC protects customers of a failed brokerage firm by helping return cash and securities held there, up to set limits, such as $500,000 per customer.

ww.Investors against any loss in value of t: SIPC does not protect against market losses; if your investments fall in value, there is no coverage, and it only helps if the brokerage fails.
ww.Bank deposits at insured banks and credi: Insuring bank deposits at banks and credit unions is done by the FDIC and the NCUA, while SIPC covers brokerage customers when a firm fails.
ww.Borrowers against rising interest rates: Protection for borrowers against rising rates and fees is not what SIPC does, because it works for brokerage customers whose firm has failed.

rw: Common stock gives its holder part ownership of the company and usually voting rights on matters such as electing the board of directors.

ww.A loan to the company issuing it: A loan to the company is what buying a bond gives, whereas common stock represents a share of ownership in the company that issues it.
ww.A guaranteed fixed rate of income: A guaranteed fixed income is a feature of bonds and some preferred stock, whereas common stock dividends are not guaranteed and can be cut.
ww.No ownership, only fixed interest: Common stock does give ownership, so saying it has none is wrong; fixed interest is what bondholders receive, not common stockholders.

rw: Preferred stock usually pays a fixed dividend, and those payments must be made before any dividends go to common stockholders, which gives it a priority.

ww.It always pays a higher dividend than an: Preferred stock does not always pay more than any bond or common stock; its dividend is fixed and varies by issue, so this claim goes too far.
ww.It gives more votes than common stock do: Preferred stock typically has no votes or fewer voting rights than common stock, so the claim that it always gives more votes is false.
ww.It cannot be sold on any exchange or mar: Preferred shares are traded on exchanges just like other stocks, so saying that they cannot be sold on any exchange is false.

rw: The coupon rate is the annual interest the bond pays, expressed as a percent of its face value, such as 5 percent of $1,000.

ww.The company's dividend yield on the stoc: A company's dividend yield on its stock is a different measure that applies to stock; a coupon rate is the interest paid on a bond.
ww.The date the bond matures and is repaid: The date a bond matures and the principal is repaid is its maturity date, and this is a different feature from the coupon rate.
ww.The price at which the bond trades each: A bond's daily market price can rise or fall with interest rates, but the coupon rate is fixed when the bond is issued and does not change.

rw: Annual interest equals the coupon rate times the face value, so 5 percent of $1,000 is 0.05 times 1,000, which equals $50 each year.

ww.$1,050: Adding the $1,000 principal to the $50 of interest gives $1,050, but that is a total payout and not the interest; 5 percent of $1,000 is $50.
ww.$500: Five hundred dollars would be 50 percent of the face value, which is ten times too large; 5 percent of $1,000 is only $50.
ww.$5: Five dollars would be 0.5 percent of $1,000, which is ten times too small; a 5 percent coupon on a $1,000 face value pays $50 each year.

rw: ETF stands for exchange-traded fund, a pooled investment that holds many securities and whose shares are bought and sold on an exchange throughout the trading day.

ww.Electronic trading firm: Electronic trading firm is not what ETF stands for, because an ETF is an investment fund that holds a basket of securities and trades like a stock.
ww.Equity transfer fee: Equity transfer fee is not the meaning of the letters ETF, which refer to a fund whose shares trade on an exchange during the day.
ww.Estimated tax form: Estimated tax form is not what ETF means; the letters stand for exchange-traded fund, an investment product and not a document for filing taxes.

rw: A call option gives its holder the right, but not the obligation, to buy a security at a set strike price before the option expires.

ww.Receive a fixed dividend each quarter fr: Receiving a fixed dividend each quarter is a feature of some stocks and not of options, which are contracts that give rights to buy or sell.
ww.Vote at shareholder meetings of the comp: Voting at shareholder meetings comes with owning shares of stock, and a call option alone gives no ownership or votes in the company.
ww.Sell a security at a set price before it: The right to sell a security at a set price before it expires belongs to a put option, which is the opposite of a call.

rw: A financial market is a place, physical or electronic, where buyers and sellers trade assets such as stocks, bonds, and currencies at prices set by supply and demand.

ww.A bank branch that only accepts deposits: A bank branch that only accepts deposits is a single institution and not a market, because a financial market is where assets are traded between buyers and sellers.
ww.A government office that collects taxes: A government office that collects taxes is a revenue agency, which does not match a financial market, where buyers and sellers trade assets such as stocks.
ww.A store where people buy groceries each: A store where people buy groceries is a retail market for goods, not a financial market, which trades financial assets like stocks and bonds.

rw: The primary market is where new securities are sold for the first time by the issuer, such as in an IPO, and the issuer receives the proceeds.

ww.The market where only bonds are traded b: Only bonds traded daily by investors does not describe the primary market, which covers new issues of any security, and trading among investors happens in the secondary market.
ww.The market where investors trade securit: Investors trading securities among themselves describes the secondary market, while the primary market is where the issuer sells new securities for the first time.
ww.The market where goods are exchanged for: Exchanging goods for goods and services is barter, which is not a financial market, and the primary market involves the first sale of new securities.

rw: The secondary market is where investors buy and sell securities that have already been issued, such as stocks traded on an exchange, and the original issuer gets no new money.

ww.The market where only the government tra: Only the government trading bonds with banks is too narrow; the secondary market is open to many investors trading all kinds of previously issued securities.
ww.The market where new securities are firs: New securities sold first by the issuer to the public describes the primary market, which is the opposite of the secondary market for previously issued securities.
ww.The market where loans are approved by l: The approval of loans by lenders is a credit decision and not a market for trading securities, so it does not describe the secondary market.

rw: A company selling new shares to the public in an IPO raises money for itself directly, which is the defining feature of a primary market transaction.

ww.A friend gives you shares as a gift on y: A gift of shares between friends is a transfer with no new securities created and no money going to the issuer, so it is not a primary transaction.
ww.An investor sells shares to another inve: One investor selling shares to another is a secondary market trade, because the shares already exist and the company receives no proceeds from the sale.
ww.A trader swaps shares through a broker f: A broker swapping shares for a client moves existing shares between owners and does not create new securities, so it takes place in the secondary market.

rw: The NYSE is a major stock exchange in New York City where shares of many large companies are listed and traded by investors.

ww.A company that issues all U.S. stocks: The NYSE does not issue stocks; companies issue their own shares, and the exchange provides the place where those shares are bought and sold.
ww.A bank owned by the state of New York: The NYSE is a private exchange company and not a bank, and it has no ownership by the state of New York.
ww.A government regulator of stocks and fun: Regulating stocks and funds is the work of the SEC, whereas the NYSE is a marketplace operating under the regulator's rules and oversight.

rw: Nasdaq is an electronic stock exchange, known for listing many technology companies, where investors buy and sell shares through a computer network instead of a trading floor.

ww.A federal agency that audits companies e: A federal agency that audits companies is not Nasdaq, which is a private electronic stock exchange where companies list their shares for trading.
ww.A bond rating agency based in New York C: A bond rating agency assesses credit risk, such as Moody's, and is a different kind of organization from Nasdaq, which is a stock exchange.
ww.A type of savings account at a local ban: A savings account at a local bank is a deposit product, and Nasdaq is a stock exchange where shares are traded, not an account type.

rw: In an OTC market, trades happen directly between dealers through a network and not on a central exchange, which is how the term is used.

ww.A market only for cash purchases at stor: OTC does not mean cash purchases at stores in a town; in finance it refers to trading securities through dealers outside a formal exchange.
ww.A market that is closed to the general p: OTC markets are open to the general public through brokers, so saying that they are closed to the public is not accurate.
ww.A market run by the SEC and the exchange: The SEC and exchanges regulate and operate many markets, but OTC trading takes place through a dealer network and is not run by them.

rw: A market index measures the performance of a group of securities, such as large companies, and gives investors a benchmark to compare the market or a portfolio.

ww.A directory of company addresses: A directory of company addresses is just a contact list and has no role in tracking market performance, which is what an index does.
ww.A rule that sets all stock prices: A market index measures performance and does not set prices, which are determined by buyers and sellers trading in the market.
ww.A list of broker fees and commissions: A list of fees and commissions is a broker's price sheet, whereas an index tracks the combined price movement of a group of securities.

rw: The S&P 500 includes about 500 large U.S. public companies, weighted by size, and it is widely used as a gauge of the U.S. stock market.

ww.Exactly 30 companies on the main list: Exactly thirty companies describes the Dow Jones Industrial Average, not the S&P 500, which has about 500 members chosen for size and stability.
ww.Only 50 companies in the whole index: Only fifty companies is too few; the number 500 is in the name of the index, and it covers about ten times that number.
ww.Exactly 5,000 companies, all listed: Five thousand companies is ten times too many for the S&P 500, which includes about 500 large U.S. public companies, and not every listed company.

rw: The Dow Jones Industrial Average follows the stock prices of 30 large, well-known U.S. companies, making it one of the oldest and most watched market indexes.

ww.Only bond prices today: Bond prices are tracked by bond indexes, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average follows the stock prices of 30 large U.S. companies.
ww.All companies on the Nasdaq: All companies on the Nasdaq are tracked by Nasdaq indexes such as the Nasdaq Composite, whereas the Dow follows only a set of 30 companies.
ww.500 large U.S. companies: Five hundred large U.S. companies are tracked by the S&P 500, which is a different index from the Dow with its much smaller list.

rw: A market maker stands ready to buy and sell a security at quoted prices, which adds liquidity so that other investors can trade easily.

ww.Issues new stock to the public each year: Issuing new stock to the public is done by the company itself with underwriters, whereas a market maker trades existing securities to keep a market going.
ww.Sets the price of every stock by law eac: No law lets a market maker set every stock's price each day; prices result from supply and demand, with market makers quoting bids and asks.
ww.Audits company books for the state agenc: Auditing company books is done by independent auditors, and market makers have no such function, since they quote prices and trade securities.

rw: The bid price is the most a buyer is currently willing to pay for a security, and it is always at or below the ask price.

ww.The price set by the government for it: The government does not set the bid price of a security; it comes from buyers who state what they are willing to pay in the market.
ww.The lowest price a seller accepts for a: The lowest price a seller will accept is the ask price, and the bid price is on the other side, as the buyer's offer.
ww.The price paid last year by the buyer: The price paid last year by a buyer is history and not a live quote, while the bid price is what buyers offer now.

rw: The ask price is the lowest price at which a seller is willing to sell a security, and buyers must pay it or higher to buy immediately.

ww.The highest price a buyer will pay for a: The highest price a buyer will pay for a share is the bid price, which is on the opposite side of the market from the ask.
ww.The price of the last tax payment made t: The last tax payment made to a state has nothing to do with securities quotes, so it cannot be the ask price of a stock.
ww.The price on the stock certificate held: The price on a stock certificate held by the first buyer is an old issue figure, not the current ask price, which changes with the market.

rw: The bid-ask spread is the gap between the highest price a buyer offers and the lowest price a seller asks, and it represents a trading cost.

ww.The difference between two companies' ea: The difference between two companies' earnings compares profits and is not the spread, which relates to the bid and ask quotes for one security.
ww.The fee a broker charges per trade made: The fee a broker charges per trade is a commission, which is separate from the spread, the gap between the bid and ask prices.
ww.The difference between a stock's high an: The difference between a stock's yearly high and low is its trading range, while the bid-ask spread is the gap between current buy and sell quotes.

rw: The spread equals the ask minus the bid, so $25.10 minus $24.90 equals $0.20, which is the gap between what buyers offer and sellers want.

ww.$0.02: Two cents would be a spread of $0.02, but the bid and ask differ by $25.10 minus $24.90, which equals $0.20, ten times larger.
ww.$25.00: Twenty-five dollars is roughly the midpoint of the bid and ask, not the spread; the spread is the ask minus the bid, which is $0.20.
ww.$50.00: Fifty dollars comes from adding the bid and the ask ($24.90 plus $25.10), but the spread is found by subtracting them, giving $0.20.

rw: Trading volume is the number of shares traded in a period, such as a day, and high volume shows strong interest and ease of buying or selling.

ww.The loudness of the trading floor today: The loudness of the trading floor is noise and not a measure used by investors; volume counts the number of shares that change hands.
ww.The number of companies on an exchange: The number of companies on an exchange is its listing count, and trading volume instead measures activity in the number of shares traded.
ww.The price of a share at the end of the d: The price of a share at the end of the day is the closing price, and volume counts how many shares were traded, not their price.

rw: Market capitalization equals the share price times the number of shares outstanding, giving the total market value of the company's equity.

ww.The number of employees a company has: The number of employees tells you about the size of the workforce and has no link to market capitalization, which is based on share price and shares outstanding.
ww.The profit a company earns each year: Profit earned each year is net income and not market cap, which values the company by the price of all its shares in the market.
ww.The total debt a company has now: The total debt a company owes is a liability on the balance sheet, and market capitalization measures the market value of its equity instead.

rw: Market cap equals shares outstanding times price, so 10 million shares times $40 equals $400 million, the total market value of the company's equity.

ww.$40 million: Forty million dollars is only the price of one million shares at $40, but there are 10 million shares, so the value is ten times larger.
ww.$4,000 million: Four thousand million dollars is ten times too big; multiplying 10 million shares by $40 gives $400 million and not $4,000 million.
ww.$4 million: Four million dollars is one hundred times too small; 10 million shares at $40 each is worth $400 million, so this answer misplaces the decimal.

rw: A large-cap stock belongs to a company with a large market capitalization, usually billions of dollars, and these firms tend to be more stable than smaller ones.

ww.A stock that is not traded on any exchan: A stock not traded on any exchange is unlisted, which has no link to size; large-cap describes a company with a large market capitalization.
ww.A stock of a company with a very small m: A company with a very small market value is a small-cap or micro-cap, which is the opposite of a large-cap stock.
ww.A stock that costs more than $100 a shar: A share price above $100 does not make a stock large-cap, since cap depends on total company value, and a small firm can have a high price.

rw: A blue-chip stock belongs to a large, sound, established company with a long record of stable earnings and often dividends, making it a reliable core holding.

ww.A stock that is blue in color and sold i: The name comes from the high-value chips in poker and has nothing to do with color or with blue chips being sold, so this is incorrect.
ww.A stock that has been banned from tradin: A stock banned from trading for a year is suspended, which is a regulatory action and says nothing about the quality of a blue-chip company.
ww.A stock of a new and unproven start-up f: A new and unproven start-up is risky and lacks a track record, which is the opposite of the established strength that blue-chip stocks show.

rw: A growth stock belongs to a company expected to increase its earnings and revenue faster than the overall market, so investors hope for price gains over time.

ww.A stock of a company that is shrinking i: A shrinking company is the opposite of a growth stock, which belongs to a firm whose earnings and sales are expected to expand quickly.
ww.A stock issued only by farms and food fi: Growth stocks are not limited to farms and food firms, because the label describes expected growth in any industry, not a farming business.
ww.A stock known for large dividends paid o: Large dividends from steady profits describe an income stock, whereas growth companies usually reinvest profits to expand and pay little or no dividend.

rw: A value stock appears to trade at a low price relative to its fundamentals, such as earnings or assets, so investors see it as a bargain.

ww.A stock that pays no attention to profit: A stock that pays no attention to profit or growth is not a value stock; value investors study fundamentals closely to find bargains.
ww.A stock that trades at a very high price: A stock trading at a very high price compared with its earnings and assets describes an expensive stock, often a growth stock, and not a value stock.
ww.A stock with no assets, no profits and n: A company with no assets, profits, or future is a failing business and not a value stock, which has a low price but sound fundamentals.
